The first hundred

By lowob · 4 March 2026 · 3-minute read · Growth

The first hundred community members are recruited, not attracted. Hand-pick them, give them real influence and close the loop on every contribution. They become your testers, your references and your first distribution channel.

Why a hundred

A hundred is small enough to know by name and large enough to generate a steady flow of feedback, referrals and public advocacy. It's also the size at which a community starts to sustain itself: members begin answering each other's questions and bringing in people you'd never have reached.

Below that, it's the founder's personal network. Above it, without the first hundred in place, it's usually an audience.

The recruitment loop

List 30 names. People whose use of the product would teach you the most or whose endorsement would mean the most: potential customers, respected builders, operators in your category, sharp critics.

Ask for judgment, not attention. "We're deciding between two approaches to X. Would you look at both and tell me which is wrong?" Specific, flattering in the right way and easy to answer.

Give the yeses a job. Early access, a test, a draft to tear apart. Something with an end date.

Close the loop in public where you can. "We changed this because Priya pointed out Y." This is the step most teams skip and the one that turns a respondent into a member.

Ask for the next name. Each person who engages is asked who else should see it. That's how 30 becomes 100 without a campaign.

This is the same mechanic as a good investor intro or a good customer referral. Give the person homework, do something visible with their answer, then ask for the next name. Run it once and it works for all three audiences.

What to give them

Access: builds, roadmaps, the founder's time.

Influence: a real decision they shaped, and evidence they shaped it.

Recognition: named in changelogs, release notes, docs credits, or onchain roles.

Each other: introduce members to one another. A community whose members know each other survives the founder getting busy.

What not to give them: vague promises of future token allocations, or anything you'd regret seeing in a screenshot.

Where to keep them

Somewhere small and owned. A private group, an email list, a feedback channel. The public server can come later. The first hundred need a room where they can be candid, and you need records you keep even if a platform changes its rules.

Web3 and AI notes

For a web3 protocol, the first hundred should include people who actually use DeFi daily, not only holders. They'll find the confusing parts of your app in minutes.

For an AI product, include at least ten people who'd pay for it. Enthusiasts give great feedback on features; buyers give great feedback on whether it's worth money.

The checklist

30 named people, written down.

A real decision to ask them about.

A small, owned space for the ones who say yes.

Every contribution acknowledged in public or in the product.

A "who else should see this?" at the end of every exchange.

lowob takeaways

  • A hundred is small enough to know by name and large enough to start sustaining itself.
  • Close the loop in public; it is the step most teams skip and turns a respondent into a member.
  • For an AI product, include at least ten people who would pay for it.
